reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard sleep & reproductive medicine references
clinicalPearls: Circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders arise from a mismatch between the internal biological clock and the desired or socially required sleep-wake schedule, so total sleep is often normal if the patient sleeps at their preferred times
Common subtypes include delayed and advanced sleep phase disorders, non-24-hour rhythm, irregular sleep-wake rhythm, and the externally imposed shift work and jet lag disorders
Delayed sleep phase disorder is typical of adolescents and young adults, who cannot fall asleep or wake at conventional times and are mislabelled as insomniacs
Advanced sleep phase disorder, with early evening sleepiness and early morning waking, is more common in older adults
Non-24-hour rhythm disorder is characteristic of totally blind people who lack light entrainment of the clock
A sleep diary, often supplemented by actigraphy, is central to demonstrating the timing pattern and confirming the diagnosis
Timed bright light exposure and appropriately scheduled melatonin, applied according to circadian principles, are the mainstays of realigning the clock
Shift work and jet lag disorders are managed with strategic light, scheduled sleep, and planned adaptation, since the environmental demand usually cannot be removed
reference.pathophysiology: The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus generates an intrinsic rhythm slightly longer than twenty-four hours that is entrained to the environment chiefly by light detected through retinal photoreceptors, with melatonin secretion providing an internal darkness signal. Circadian rhythm disorders occur when this clock is misaligned with the external day. Intrinsic disorders reflect altered clock timing or entrainment: a long intrinsic period or reduced morning light sensitivity delays the phase, an advanced phase shortens it, absent light input (blindness) causes free-running non-24-hour rhythms, and weakened clock output produces an irregular rhythm as seen in neurodegenerative disease. Extrinsic disorders (shift work, jet lag) arise when behaviour and light exposure are acutely forced out of step with the still-entrained internal clock, producing sleepiness, insomnia, and impaired performance until re-entrainment occurs.
additionalDifferentials: Depression or other mood disorder affecting sleep timing
Substance or medication effects on sleep-wake timing
Neurodegenerative disease with irregular sleep-wake rhythm
additionalInvestigations: Detailed sleep-wake history with a prospective sleep diary over one to two weeks
Actigraphy to objectively document sleep-wake timing patterns
Assessment of light exposure, work schedule, and travel history
Where available, markers of circadian phase such as dim-light melatonin onset
Screening for coexisting mood disorder or other sleep pathology
redFlags: Sleepiness during shift work causing accidents or dangerous errors
Irregular sleep-wake rhythm emerging with cognitive decline, suggesting neurodegenerative disease
Severe social, educational, or occupational impairment from persistent misalignment
Coexisting depression with the circadian disturbance
reference.prognosis: Intrinsic disorders such as delayed sleep phase can usually be improved with disciplined light and melatonin timing, though relapse is common if the regimen lapses; shift work and jet lag disorders resolve with adaptation or cessation of the schedule, and outcomes are poorer when the environmental demand cannot be altered.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing delayed sleep phase disorder as primary insomnia and prescribing hypnotics
Giving light or melatonin at the wrong circadian time and worsening the misalignment
Overlooking blindness as the cause of a free-running non-24-hour rhythm
Ignoring the occupational safety consequences of shift work sleepiness
management: Appropriately timed bright light exposure to shift and entrain the clock, with morning light for delayed sleep phase and evening light for advanced sleep phase
Timed melatonin to reinforce phase shifting, and a melatonin-receptor agonist such as tasimelteon for non-24-hour rhythm disorder in blind patients
Structured sleep-wake scheduling, sleep hygiene and chronotherapy to consolidate the desired sleep timing
For shift work, planned napping, strategic caffeine and timed light, with a wake-promoting agent such as modafinil for excessive sleepiness; for jet lag, timed light and melatonin
A prospective sleep diary and actigraphy to document timing and to guide and monitor treatment
Screening for and treatment of coexisting mood disorder or other sleep pathology
Referral to a sleep medicine service for refractory or complex cases
